units.title: Hello, Lisp
units.summary: Write your first Lisp program, print text with format and calculate with prefix notation.

lesson.md: Common Lisp is one of the oldest programming languages that people still use today. A Lisp program is a series of **forms**. A form in parentheses is a call: the first element names the operator, and the other elements are its arguments. This program prints one line:

`format` prints text. Its first argument is the destination: `t` means the screen (the standard output). The second argument is the text in double quotes, called a **string**. Inside it, `~%` starts a new line. A semicolon `;` starts a comment, which Lisp ignores until the end of the line.

In Lisp, the operator always comes first: you write `(+ 2 3)` instead of `2 + 3`. This is called **prefix notation**. A form like this, with parentheses around it, is also called an **s-expression** (symbolic expression). `+` and `*` accept any number of arguments, and `-` and `/` work the same way.

To print a value, put `~a` into the string. `format` replaces each `~a` with the next argument after the string. Forms can be nested: Lisp evaluates the inner form first, so `(* 2 (+ 3 4))` becomes `(* 2 7)` and then `14`.

lesson.code:
(format t "~a~%" (+ 2 3))
(format t "~a~%" (+ 1 2 3 4))
(format t "~a~%" (* 2 (+ 3 4)))
(format t "~a plus ~a is ~a~%" 2 3 (+ 2 3))

lesson.md: `~s` also inserts a value, but it shows it the way Lisp reads it, so a string keeps its double quotes. The function `print` shows a value in the same way. It writes a new line first, then the value, then a space. That is why this course mostly uses `format` for clean output.
Every opening parenthesis needs a closing one. Most Lisp editors show you which parentheses belong together, and programmers read Lisp code by its indentation.

card: `(format t "Hi~%")` prints `Hi` and a new line
`~a` inserts the next argument, `~s` keeps quotes
`(print x)` new line, value with quotes, space

exercises.explain: `(+ 4 5)` adds 4 and 5, and `~a` puts the result into the text.
The inner form `(+ 1 4)` is 5. Then `(* 2 5)` is 10.
In Lisp the operator always comes first, inside the parentheses.
The first string has no `~%`, so no new line follows `Hi`. The second text continues on the same line.

exercises.explain: `~%` is the directive for a new line. Without it, the next output continues on the same line.

units.title: Values
units.summary: Work with numbers, exact ratios, strings, symbols, t and nil, and name values with defparameter.

lesson.md: Lisp has whole numbers (integers) like `42` and decimal numbers (floats) like `2.5`. Integers can be as large as you need. `expt` raises a number to a power, so `(expt 2 100)` is 2 to the power of 100.

When you divide two integers and the result is not whole, Lisp gives an exact fraction called a **ratio**: `(/ 10 4)` is `5/2`. If one number is a float, the result is a float. `mod` gives the remainder of a division: `(mod 17 5)` is `2`.
A string is text in double quotes. `length` counts its characters, and `string-upcase` returns it in capital letters. `(concatenate 'string "a" "b")` joins strings into one new string.

A **symbol** is a name. The quote `'` tells Lisp: do not evaluate this, take it as it is. So `'apple` is the symbol `APPLE`. Lisp turns symbol names into capital letters when it reads them, so they print in capitals. In `concatenate`, the symbol `'string` says what kind of result you want.

Lisp writes true as `t` and false as `nil`. Comparisons return one of them: `>` (greater than), `<` (less than), `>=`, `<=` and `=` (equal numbers). `(< 1 2 3)` checks that each number is smaller than the next. Functions that answer a yes or no question often end in `p`, like `stringp` (is it a string?). Every value except `nil` counts as true.

`(defparameter *price* 12)` creates a global variable named `*price*` with the value `12`. The stars around the name are a convention for global variables. Names can contain hyphens, like `*max-speed*`.
Because Lisp turns names into capital letters, `*Price*` and `*price*` are the same variable. Most Lisp programmers write all code in lowercase.

exercises.explain: 12 divided by 8 is not whole, so Lisp gives the exact ratio `3/2`.
6 fits into 20 three times (18), and the remainder is 2.
The quote makes `hello` a symbol. Lisp stores symbol names in capital letters.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Define your own functions with defun, use parameters and return values, and write functions without a name.

lesson.md: `defun` defines a function. After `defun` comes the name, then a list of **parameters** in parentheses, then the body. A function returns the value of the last form in its body. Lisp needs no `return` keyword.
A function can have several parameters. You call your own functions like the built-in ones: the name first, then the arguments.
The body can contain several forms. Lisp runs them in order, but only the value of the last one is returned. Here the function prints a greeting and returns the length of the name.
Functions can call other functions. A function without parameters has an empty list `()`.

lesson.code:
(defun twice (n)
  (* 2 n))

(defun four-times (n)
  (twice (twice n)))

(defun say-hello ()
  (format t "Hello!~%"))

(say-hello)
(format t "~a~%" (four-times 5))

lesson.md: `(lambda (x) (* x 10))` creates a function without a name. It has a parameter list and a body, like `defun`. You can call it directly by putting it first in a form. In the unit about higher-order functions, you pass such functions to other functions.

lesson.code:
(format t "~a~%" ((lambda (x) (* x 10)) 4))
(format t "~a~%" ((lambda (a b) (+ a b)) 2 3))

lesson.md: Lisp programmers write names in lowercase with hyphens between words, like `four-times` or `celsius-to-fahrenheit`.
A call needs exactly as many arguments as the function has parameters. `(square 2 3)` stops the program with an error.

card: `(defun name (a b) body)` defines a function
The last form of the body is the return value

exercises.explain: `triple` multiplies its argument by 3, and 3 times 7 is 21.
The arguments go into the parameters in order: `a` is 3 and `b` is 10, so the result is `(- 3 10)`.
Both forms run, but only the value of the last form, `(+ x 1)`, is returned.

exercises.explain: A function returns the value of the last form in its body automatically.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program choose with if, when, unless and cond, and combine tests with and, or and not.

lesson.md: `(if test then else)` has three parts. When the test is true (anything except `nil`), Lisp evaluates the `then` form. Otherwise it evaluates the `else` form.
`if` returns a value, like every form in Lisp. You can use it inside other forms, for example as the body of a function.

`when` runs its body only when the test is true. `unless` runs its body only when the test is false. Both can contain several forms, but they have no `else` part. When the body does not run, they return `nil`.

`cond` checks several clauses in order. Each clause is a list: a test, then the result. Only the first clause whose test is true runs. A last clause with the test `t` is always true, so it catches all other cases.

lesson.code:
(defun grade (score)
  (cond ((>= score 90) "A")
        ((>= score 70) "B")
        (t "C")))

(format t "~a~%" (grade 95))
(format t "~a~%" (grade 75))
(format t "~a~%" (grade 40))

lesson.md: `(and a b)` is true when all its arguments are true, and `(or a b)` when at least one is. `and` returns the last value, `or` returns the first value that is not `nil`. `(not x)` turns `nil` into `T` and every other value into `NIL`. `evenp` and `oddp` check whether a number is even or odd.

lesson.code:
(defun even-and-positive (n)
  (and (> n 0) (evenp n)))

(format t "~a~%" (even-and-positive 4))
(format t "~a~%" (even-and-positive 7))
(format t "~a~%" (or nil 5))
(format t "~a~%" (not nil))

lesson.md: `=` compares only numbers. To compare strings, use `equal`: `(equal "yes" "yes")` is `T`.

card: `(if test then else)` returns a value
`(cond (test1 a) (test2 b) (t c))` first true clause

2 is not greater than 5. So `when` does not run its body, but `unless` does.

exercises.explain: Only `nil` is false. `0` is a normal value, so it counts as true.

units.title: Lists
units.summary: Build lists with list and cons, take them apart with first and rest, and join them with append.

lesson.md: A list holds values in order. `(list 1 2 3)` creates a list. You can also write a list with a quote: `'(1 2 3)`. The quote stops Lisp from treating the list as a call. With `~a`, a list prints in parentheses.

`first` returns the first element. `rest` returns a list of all the other elements. The older names `car` and `cdr` do the same, and you see them often in Lisp code. `(nth 2 list)` returns the element at position 2, counting from 0.

`cons` puts a value in front of a list and returns the new list. Inside, a list is a chain of **cons cells**: each cell holds one value (the `car`) and the rest of the list (the `cdr`). The empty list is `nil`, which you can also write as `()`.

lesson.code:
(format t "~a~%" (cons 0 '(1 2 3)))
(format t "~a~%" (cons 1 nil))
(format t "~a~%" (rest '(5)))
(format t "~a~%" (cons 1 (cons 2 (cons 3 nil))))

lesson.md: `length` counts the elements. `append` joins lists into one, and `reverse` returns the elements in the opposite order. `null` checks whether a list is empty.
`cons`, `append` and `reverse` do not change the original list. They return a new list.
Without a quote, `(1 2 3)` is a call: Lisp tries to use `1` as a function and stops with an error. Write `'(1 2 3)` or `(list 1 2 3)`.

exercises.explain: `rest` returns `(20 30)`, and its first element is 20.

The list has only one element, so the rest is the empty list, `NIL`.
`car` is the old name of `first`. Both return the first element of a list.

units.title: Higher-order functions
units.summary: Pass functions to other functions: transform lists with mapcar, filter with remove-if-not and combine with reduce.

lesson.md: In Lisp, functions are values. `#'square` means the function named `square`; it is short for `(function square)`. A function that takes other functions as arguments is called a **higher-order function**.
`mapcar` calls a function on every element of a list and returns a new list with the results.
Often you pass a `lambda` instead of a named function. With two lists, `mapcar` takes one element from each list for every call.
`remove-if-not` keeps only the elements for which the test function returns true. `remove-if` does the opposite: it removes them.

`reduce` combines all elements into one value with a function of two arguments. `(reduce #'+ '(1 2 3 4))` first adds 1 and 2, then adds 3 to the result, then 4. `max` returns the largest of its arguments.
`funcall` calls a function that you have as a value, for example in a parameter. With it, you can write your own higher-order functions. `1+` adds one to a number.

lesson.code:
(defun apply-twice (f x)
  (funcall f (funcall f x)))

(format t "~a~%" (apply-twice #'1+ 5))
(format t "~a~%" (apply-twice (lambda (n) (* n 3)) 2))

lesson.md: Lisp keeps the names of functions and variables apart. That is why you need `#'` to pass a function, and `funcall` to call a function stored in a variable.

card: `(mapcar f list)` applies `f` to every element
`(funcall f x)` calls a function value

`mapcar` collects the result of `evenp` for each element. It does not filter.
`mapcar` returns a new list. The original list stays the same.

units.title: Iteration and recursion
units.summary: Repeat code with dotimes, dolist and loop, and solve problems with functions that call themselves.

lesson.md: `(dotimes (i 3) body)` runs the body 3 times. The variable `i` counts from `0` up to, but not including, `3`.
`(dolist (x list) body)` runs the body once for every element of a list. Each time, `x` holds the next element.

lesson.output:
I like apple.
I like pear.
I like plum.

lesson.md: `loop` is a small language of its own. `for i from 1 to 5` counts from 1 to 5, including both ends, and `for i below 3` counts from 0 to 2. `for x in list` goes through a list. `collect` builds a list of values, `sum` adds them up, and `do` runs forms. `downto` counts down.

lesson.code:
(format t "~a~%" (loop for i from 1 to 5 collect (* i i)))
(format t "~a~%" (loop for i below 3 collect i))
(format t "~a~%" (loop for x in '(3 4 5) sum x))
(loop for i from 10 downto 8
      do (format t "~a~%" i))

lesson.md: A **recursive** function calls itself. It needs a **base case**, a simple case that it answers without calling itself. The factorial of `n` is `n` times the factorial of `n - 1`, and the factorial of 1 is 1.

lesson.code:
(defun factorial (n)
  (if (<= n 1)
      1
      (* n (factorial (- n 1)))))

(format t "~a~%" (factorial 5))
(format t "~a~%" (factorial 20))

lesson.md: Recursion fits lists well: handle the first element, call the function again on the rest, and stop at the empty list. `null` checks for the empty list.
Without a base case, a recursive function calls itself again and again until the program stops with an error.

card: `(loop for i from 1 to 5 collect i)`, also `sum`, `do`
Recursion: base case first, then call with a smaller value

units.title: Local variables and data
units.summary: Use local variables with let, change values with setf, and store data in hash tables and structures.

lesson.md: `let` creates **local variables**. They exist only inside the body of the `let`. The first part is a list of pairs: a name and its value.
`let` creates all its variables at the same time, so one value cannot use another variable of the same `let`. `let*` creates them one after another, so later values can use earlier ones.
`setf` gives a variable a new value. `incf` adds 1 to a variable, or the number you give it.

lesson.code:
(let ((x 5))
  (setf x (* x 2))
  (format t "~a~%" x))

(defun count-even (numbers)
  (let ((result 0))
    (dolist (n numbers)
      (when (evenp n)
        (incf result)))
    result))

(format t "~a~%" (count-even '(1 2 4 6 7)))

lesson.md: A **hash table** stores values under keys. `(make-hash-table :test #'equal)` creates one. Words that start with a colon, like `:test`, are **keywords**; they name an argument. `:test #'equal` lets you use strings as keys. `(gethash key table)` reads a value, and `(setf (gethash key table) value)` stores one. A missing key gives `NIL`, or the default value you pass as a third argument. `incf` also works on `(gethash key table 0)`, which makes counting easy. `hash-table-count` counts the entries.

`defstruct` defines a new kind of record with named fields. `(defstruct point x y)` creates the function `make-point`, the readers `point-x` and `point-y`, and the test `point-p`. You give the field values with keywords, like `:x 3`. `setf` also changes a field.

lesson.code:
(defstruct point x y)

(defparameter *p* (make-point :x 3 :y 4))
(format t "~a~%" (point-x *p*))
(setf (point-y *p*) 10)
(format t "~a ~a~%" (point-x *p*) (point-y *p*))
(format t "~a~%" (point-p *p*))

lesson.md: A variable from `let` does not exist outside the `let`. Using it there stops the program with an error.

card: `(gethash key table)` read, `(setf (gethash key table) v)` store

`let` creates its variables at the same time, so `a` does not exist yet when `b` is computed. With `let*` it would print `2`.
